title: YOU WERE TOLD, “GIVE AND GOD WILL GIVE YOU MORE”—BUT WHAT IF JESUS WAS TALKING ABOUT SOMETHING FAR DEEPER?
paragraphs: YOU WERE TOLD, “GIVE AND GOD WILL GIVE YOU MORE”—BUT WHAT IF JESUS WAS TALKING ABOUT SOMETHING FAR DEEPER?
Understanding “Give and It Will Be Given to You” Without Turning God Into an Investment Plan—and discovering the scandalous grace hidden inside one of Christianity’s most misunderstood promises.
There is a dangerous way to read the Bible that can make God sound less like a Father and more like an investment opportunity.
Put something in.
Wait for the return.
Give $100.
Believe for $1,000.
Plant a “seed.”
Expect a financial harvest.
And somewhere along the way, a breathtaking statement from the lips of Jesus can be reduced to something resembling a heavenly transaction:
“Give, and it will be given to you.”
It sounds convincing when those words are isolated.
It sounds even more convincing when the rest of the verse is quoted:
“Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, will be put into your bosom.”
Luke 6:38.
That sounds like abundance.
Overflow.
Multiplication.
And it is.
But there is a question we desperately need to ask before building a theology of money around it:
What was Jesus actually talking about?
Because if we love Jesus, we cannot merely ask what a verse can be made to say.
We must ask what Jesus meant.
And what happens when we put Luke 6:38 back where Jesus put it may surprise you.
It may even expose something in us.
Because immediately before saying, “Give, and it will be given to you,” Jesus says:
“Judge not, and you shall not be judged. Condemn not, and you shall not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”
Then comes:
“Give, and it will be given to you.”
Read that slowly.
Jesus has been talking about mercy.
Judgment.
Condemnation.
Forgiveness.
Generosity.
The way human beings treat one another.
And the larger sermon makes His point even more uncomfortable.
Jesus says:
“Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, and pray for those who spitefully use you.”
Then:
“Love your enemies, do good, and lend, hoping for nothing in return.”
Luke 6:35.
And then He gives the reason:
“Therefore be merciful, just as your Father also is merciful.”
Luke 6:36.
That changes everything.
Jesus is not standing behind a heavenly cash register saying, “Give Me enough money and I will make you rich.”
He is revealing what people transformed by the mercy of God begin to look like.
They give.
They forgive.
They show mercy.
They release condemnation.
They love people who cannot repay them.
They lend without making repayment the center of their kindness.
They become generous because their Father is generous.
The Greek makes the statement beautifully direct:
δίδοτε, καὶ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν
didote, kai dothēsetai hymin
“Give, and it will be given to you.”
The first word, δίδοτε — didote, comes from didōmi, “to give.”
It is an imperative.
Jesus really is commanding generosity.
We should not weaken that.
Christianity is not permission to clutch everything God places in our hands.
But notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not provide an investment percentage.
He does not promise that every dollar donated will return as multiple dollars.
He does not turn generosity into a technique for controlling Providence.
In fact, only a few sentences earlier He tells His disciples to lend while “hoping for nothing in return.”
That is devastating to transactional Christianity.
Jesus is teaching generosity that can survive even when there is nothing in it for you.
And perhaps that is exactly where this teaching begins to hurt.
Because many of us are willing to give...
as long as God pays us back the way we want.
We will obey if the marriage improves.
Serve if somebody notices.
Forgive if they apologize.
Give if our finances increase.
Pray if the breakthrough arrives.
Remain faithful if life starts making sense.
But what happens when you give and the bank account does not suddenly overflow?
What happens when you forgive and the person never says sorry?
What happens when you serve and nobody applauds?
What happens when you obey God and your circumstances become harder?
What happens when the “return” you expected never arrives?
Does God still deserve your obedience?
That question reaches much deeper than money.
It reaches the hidden contract many of us have attempted to write with God.
“Lord, I will give You this...
if You give me that.”
And Jesus quietly tears up the contract.
Because grace was never a business transaction.
The Gospel itself proves it.
God did not look down at humanity and find spiritually wealthy customers worthy of an investment.
He found sinners.
Rebels.
The guilty.
The ashamed.
The self-righteous.
The sexually broken.
The greedy.
The bitter.
The religious hypocrite hiding behind respectable clothes.
The person who promised God, “Never again,” and returned to the same sin three days later.
People like us.
And Scripture says:
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8.
Before you could repay Him.
Before you could impress Him.
Before you cleaned yourself up.
Before you had anything worthy to place on the table...
Christ came.
That is grace.
Scandalous grace.
The innocent One stood where the guilty belonged.
Jesus Christ carried sin to the cross, suffered, died, and rose again so that sinners who repent and trust in Him could be forgiven and reconciled to God.
Christian generosity begins there.
Not with:
“How much can I get?”
But:
“How much have I already received in Christ?”
Forgiveness you could never purchase.
Mercy you could never earn.
Adoption you could never deserve.
A Savior you could never repay.
Eternal life you could never afford.
And suddenly giving changes.
You are no longer putting coins into heaven hoping God’s machine spits out prosperity.
You are opening hands that were already filled by grace.
This does not mean Scripture separates God from material provision.
It does not.
Jesus taught us to pray:
“Give us day by day our daily bread.”
Luke 11:3.
Paul tells us that God is able to provide sufficiently so believers can abound in good works, and he connects generosity with thanksgiving to God in 2 Corinthians 9:6–11.
Philippians 4:19 declares:
“And my God shall supply all your need according to His riches in glory by Christ Jesus.”
God provides.
God cares.
God owns everything.
God can bless materially.
God can open doors nobody else can open.
God can provide through work, generosity, community, circumstances, and means we never anticipated.
But biblical provision is not the same thing as turning God into an investment plan.
There is an enormous difference between trusting the Father to provide and attempting to manipulate the Father through giving.
One says:
“Father, everything I possess belongs to You.”
The other says:
“God, I gave You something. Now You owe me.”
One is worship.
The other is leverage wearing religious clothing.
And God will not be reduced to leverage.
There is another beautiful detail in Luke 6:38.
Jesus describes the measure as:
μέτρον καλὸν πεπιεσμένον σεσαλευμένον ὑπερεκχυννόμενον
A good measure—pressed down, shaken together, running over.
The picture is vivid.
Imagine dry goods being measured into a container. The contents are pressed and shaken so empty spaces disappear, then more is poured until the measure overflows.
Jesus gives His listeners a picture they could feel.
Abundance.
Generosity without stinginess.
Then comes the principle:
“For with the same measure that you use, it will be measured back to you.”
But even here, we must resist forcing Jesus into a simplistic formula.
This is not a divine vending machine.
The Bible itself refuses that interpretation.
Consider the apostle Paul.
If faithfulness automatically produced material prosperity, Paul should have been extraordinarily wealthy.
Instead, he describes hunger, thirst, cold, nakedness, beatings, imprisonment, danger, and hardship.
Consider Jesus Himself.
He lived without the luxurious earthly prosperity some modern preaching implies every faithful believer should expect.
The cross alone destroys the idea that obedience always produces immediate comfort.
Sometimes obedience costs you.
Sometimes faithfulness empties the room.
Sometimes telling the truth loses the opportunity.
Sometimes refusing corruption costs money.
Sometimes generosity means you possess less afterward.
Sometimes following Jesus leads through suffering before resurrection.
And still...
He is worthy.
This is where “give and it will be given to you” becomes far more beautiful than a promise of easy money.
Jesus is forming a people whose lives reflect their Father.
People who do not merely calculate what others deserve.
People who know how much mercy they themselves needed.
People whose hands stay open because grace opened their hearts.
Maybe you know what it feels like to need that kind of mercy.
Maybe there is something you have never told anybody.
A failure buried beneath church clothes.
A private addiction.
A relationship you destroyed.
Money you mishandled.
A betrayal.
A secret habit.
A season when you ran from God so aggressively that you wondered whether there was any road back.
Maybe people remember your scandal.
Maybe you remember it every morning.
And shame keeps whispering:
“You cannot become what God wanted anymore.”
But shame does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
Peter denied Him.
A thief was dying beside Him.
Paul once persecuted His church.
The Corinthian believers had histories Scripture itself describes with shocking honesty.
Yet the Gospel repeatedly shows God taking ruined stories and writing redemption across them.
Not because sin does not matter.
Sin matters enough that Christ went to the cross.
Repentance matters.
Holiness matters.
Truth matters.
But grace means your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when Jesus Christ becomes Lord of your story.
That is why we say:
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
He does something greater.
He redeems sinners.
He forgives the repentant.
He restores the broken.
He transforms people from the inside out.
He takes hands that once grabbed...
and teaches them to give.
He takes hearts that once condemned...
and teaches them mercy.
He takes people drowning in unforgiveness...
and reminds them of the cross where their own impossible debt was answered by grace.
Perhaps the greatest evidence that you understand “give and it will be given to you” is not the size of your bank account.
Perhaps it is what grace has done to your heart.
Can you give when nobody applauds?
Can you serve when nobody posts your name?
Can you help someone who cannot advance your career?
Can you forgive without pretending the wound was acceptable?
Can you bless someone without secretly calculating what you will receive?
Can you give because Christ has already become your treasure?
That is freedom.
Money stops being your master.
Possessions stop being your identity.
Giving stops being gambling with God.
Generosity becomes worship.
And yes, faithful Christian ministries need support.
Books need to be written.
Resources need to be created.
The Gospel needs to be proclaimed.
Believers need discipleship.
People drowning in darkness need someone willing to carry the light into places where despair has become normal.
But hear this carefully:
Do not give because somebody frightened you into believing your blessing depends on paying us.
Do not support any Christian ministry because you believe your money purchases favor from God.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot purchase salvation.
You cannot bribe God into blessing you.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Support Gospel Warrior because you believe Christ should be proclaimed.
Support because biblical truth should travel farther than deception.
Support because somebody scrolling Facebook at 2:13 in the morning, exhausted, ashamed, spiritually numb, and seconds away from giving up may encounter words that point them back to Jesus.
But the discount is not the reason to stand with us.
Christ is.
And there is another way you can help that costs nothing.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
They need to know:
God's grace is not for sale.
And if this exposed something hidden in your own relationship with God, do not hide behind silence.
Someone else reading the comments may realize they are not the only person learning this.
Because eventually you will hear Luke 6:38 quoted again.
And when you do, come back.
Read the verses around it.
Remember the mercy.
Remember the enemies Jesus told us to love.
Remember the forgiveness.
Remember the command to lend expecting nothing in return.
Remember the Father whose generosity His children are called to imitate.
Because the world does not merely need Christians who know how to quote Bible verses.
It needs Christians willing to let the Bible correct them.
Christians whose generosity cannot be purchased by applause.
Christians whose mercy confuses a cruel world.
Christians who give without turning God into a debtor.
Christians who understand that the greatest gift they ever received did not arrive because they planted enough money.
It arrived while they were sinners.
At a cross.
Outside Jerusalem.
Where the Son of God stretched out His hands.
Empty.
Wounded.
Pierced.
Giving Himself.
And perhaps that is the image we should remember whenever someone asks what Christian giving ultimately looks like.
Not a clenched fist demanding return.
Open hands.
A surrendered life.
A crucified Savior.
Jesus did not die so we could discover a religious technique for becoming rich.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
He rose so death would not have the final word.
And when His grace captures a human heart, something astonishing begins to happen.
The person who once asked,
“What can I get?”
slowly begins asking,
“Lord, what can I give?”
Not to purchase His love.
Because His love has already changed them.
Not to earn salvation.
Because salvation is by grace.
Not to manipulate tomorrow.
Because tomorrow belongs to Him.
But because once you understand what happened at Calvary...
you stop treating God like an investment.
You start treating Him like your King.
So give.
Give generously.
Give wisely.
Give joyfully.
Give to those in need.
Give toward faithful Gospel work.
Give your time.
Give encouragement.
Give forgiveness.
Give mercy.
Give without worshiping the return.
And above everything else...
give yourself to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Trust the One who gave Himself for sinners.
Because eventually every earthly account closes.
Every possession changes hands.
Every investment stays behind.
Every human body returns to dust.
And on that day, the question will not be how cleverly you turned religion into profit.
The question that matters eternally is whether you belong to Christ.
And maybe that is what your heart needed to hear today.
You were never meant to use Jesus to obtain your treasure—Jesus Himself is the Treasure.
